subject: Neurology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with a history of alcoholism is admitted with severe hyponatremia (sodium 110 mEq/L). Over 12 hours his sodium is corrected to 140 mEq/L with hypertonic saline. Two days later he develops acute flaccid paralysis, dysarthria, and dysphagia.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Osmotic demyelination syndrome, also called central pontine myelinolysis, causes massive axonal demyelination in pontine white matter from rapid osmotic shifts, most commonly overly rapid correction of hyponatremia. It produces acute paralysis, dysarthria, dysphagia, diplopia, and altered consciousness. The teaching is from low to high, your pons will die.

explanation_incorrect.A: Guillain-Barre syndrome causes symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia and albuminocytologic dissociation, without a relationship to sodium correction.
explanation_incorrect.B: Wernicke encephalopathy presents with confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia from thiamine deficiency, not acute paralysis after sodium correction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is a multifocal post-infectious demyelination with altered mental status, not a pontine lesion from osmotic shifts.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis causes episodic weakness related to potassium shifts, not iatrogenic sodium correction.

educationalObjective: Associate rapid correction of hyponatremia with central pontine myelinolysis and acute bulbar and motor deficits.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 24-year-old man develops symmetric weakness and tingling in both feet 10 days after a diarrheal illness. The weakness has ascended to his knees and he can no longer walk. Deep tendon reflexes are absent, and he has mild bilateral facial weakness.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is the most common subtype of Guillain-Barre syndrome. It destroys Schwann cells in motor and sensory peripheral nerves, often after molecular mimicry triggered by Campylobacter jejuni or viral infection. It produces symmetric ascending weakness with absent reflexes, facial paralysis, and potential respiratory failure.

explanation_incorrect.B: Multiple sclerosis is a CNS demyelinating disease with upper motor neuron signs and optic or brainstem findings, not an ascending areflexic neuropathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acute intermittent porphyria presents with abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and dark urine rather than symmetric ascending areflexia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Botulism causes a descending flaccid paralysis with dilated fixed pupils and autonomic findings, not an ascending pattern after diarrhea.
explanation_incorrect.E: Spinal cord compression produces a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs below the lesion rather than symmetric ascending areflexia.

educationalObjective: Recognize the symmetric ascending weakness and areflexia of post-infectious Guillain-Barre syndrome.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive symmetric ascending weakness and absent deep tendon reflexes. Her vital capacity is decreasing. CSF analysis shows elevated protein with a normal cell count.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying treatment?

options.text: Plasma exchange is contraindicated in this condition

explanation_correct: This is Guillain-Barre syndrome with albuminocytologic dissociation, elevated CSF protein with a normal cell count. Disease-modifying treatment is with plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, and respiratory support is critical until recovery. Steroids have no role in Guillain-Barre syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barre syndrome and are explicitly not indicated.
explanation_incorrect.B: Plasma exchange is not contraindicated; it is one of the two established disease-modifying therapies for Guillain-Barre syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acetazolamide lowers intracranial pressure in idiopathic intracranial hypertension and does not treat acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Beta-interferon is a disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis, not Guillain-Barre syndrome.

educationalObjective: Select IVIG or plasma exchange and recognize the no-steroids rule in Guillain-Barre syndrome.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 6-year-old boy develops rapidly progressive multifocal neurologic symptoms including weakness, ataxia, and altered mental status 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. MRI shows multiple large demyelinating lesions.
question: Which of the following best describes this condition?

options.text: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis following infection or vaccination

explanation_correct: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is multifocal inflammation and demyelination that follows an infection or vaccination. It presents with rapidly progressive multifocal neurologic symptoms and altered mental status, classically in children, and MRI shows multiple large demyelinating lesions. It is a post-infectious, monophasic illness.

explanation_incorrect.A: Multiple sclerosis is a relapsing-remitting CNS disease of young adults rather than an acute post-infectious monophasic illness in a child.
explanation_incorrect.C: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy results from JC virus reactivation with severe immunosuppression and is usually fatal.
explanation_incorrect.D: Osmotic demyelination syndrome is a pontine lesion caused by rapid correction of hyponatremia, not a post-infectious multifocal process.
explanation_incorrect.E: Guillain-Barre syndrome is a peripheral ascending areflexic neuropathy without the multifocal CNS lesions and altered mental status seen here.

educationalObjective: Identify ADEM as a post-infectious multifocal demyelination with altered mental status in children.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has had difficulty running and frequent ankle sprains since childhood. Examination shows pes cavus deformity, hammer toes, and foot drop. He has decreased vibration sense and proprioception in his feet. His father has similar foot deformities.
question: Which of the following is the most likely genetic cause?

options.text: CTP repeat expansion in the DM1 gene
Point mutation in the CFTR gene

explanation_correct: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy that is typically autosomal dominant and causes foot deformities such as pes cavus and hammer toe, lower extremity weakness with foot drop, and sensory loss of vibration and proprioception. The most common type, CMT1A, is caused by PMP22 gene duplication, remembered as Can't Move Toes.

explanation_incorrect.A: NF1 mutation causes neurofibromatosis type 1 with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not a distal hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy.
explanation_incorrect.B: A CTG repeat expansion in DM1 causes myotonic dystrophy with myotonia and systemic features, not the CMT foot deformity phenotype.
explanation_incorrect.C: SMN1 mutation causes spinal muscular atrophy, a pure motor neuron disease without the sensory deficits of CMT.
explanation_incorrect.D: CFTR mutation causes cystic fibrosis and is not associated with a peripheral hereditary neuropathy.

educationalObjective: Link PMP22 duplication in CMT1A to pes cavus, foot drop, and distal sensory loss.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 42-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 40 cells/µL develops rapidly progressive visual loss and right-sided weakness over several weeks. MRI shows demyelinating lesions in the parietal and occipital regions.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.text: Reactivation of latent JC virus causing oligodendrocyte destruction
Campylobacter jejuni infection triggering molecular mimicry

explanation_correct: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by reactivation of latent JC virus with destruction of oligodendrocytes in the setting of severe immunosuppression such as AIDS, leukemia or lymphoma, transplantation, or natalizumab therapy. It predominantly involves parietal and occipital regions with visual symptoms and is rapidly progressive and usually fatal.

explanation_incorrect.B: Autoimmune demyelination with oligoclonal bands describes multiple sclerosis, which occurs in immunocompetent young women rather than severely immunocompromised patients.
explanation_incorrect.C: Herpes simplex virus encephalitis typically affects the temporal lobes with fever and seizures rather than parietal and occipital demyelination.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rapid correction of hyponatremia causes central pontine myelinolysis in the pons, not multifocal parietal and occipital lesions.
explanation_incorrect.E: Campylobacter jejuni molecular mimicry causes Guillain-Barre syndrome, a peripheral neuropathy, not CNS demyelination.

educationalObjective: Recognize JC virus reactivation causing fatal parietal and occipital demyelination in severe immunosuppression.
